utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May we first hear the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland assisted by Lise-Lotte Karlsson, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. We can read on the scheduling order for today the word "deliberation." This is not foreseen in the rules, but nevertheless, it emanates from the duty of the Chamber to hear the parties, and especially to grant the right to be heard for the Prosecutor in case the Chamber believes that it might come to the conclusion that an acquittal in part is the correct reaction. And therefore, in order to address these issues and to give the parties the possibilities to give oral submissions, also on legal issues or on factual issues, and to streamline the case and to concentrate on the core issues, this was the first intention when we decided to have this meeting on deliberations today. Unfortunately, the situation has slightly changed with a view to the development in the last weeks. You know that we have to be aware that it might be that in the next -- in the near future, the Trial Chamber can no longer act in the same composition as it is now. Therefore, let me please, and it has also for the transcript, to be stated that this question was discussed in the framework of a 65 ter (I) meeting last week, how to proceed in the case. And if the situation arises that, as it is stated -- as you can read it in Rule 15 bis (C), "If a Judge is, for any reason, unable to continue sitting in a part-heard case for a period which is likely to be longer than of a short duration, the Presiding Judge shall report to the President who may assign another Judge to the case and order either a rehearing or continuation of the proceedings from that point. However, after the opening statements provided for in Rule 84, or the beginning of the presentation of evidence pursuant to Rule 85, the continuation of the proceedings can only be ordered with the consent of the accused." As mentioned before, the Defence has had the possibility to discuss this issue before the last 65 ter (I) meeting with the client, and at the same time they asked for an additional period of time to discuss this issue with the client this morning. Dr. Stakic, may I ask you, are you prepared by way of precaution that in case a judge in this Chamber, to be concrete, Judge Fassi Fihri, would or will be unable to continue sitting in this part-heard case, to express your unconditioned and irrevocable consent to continue with the proceedings? First of all, did you understand what is the meaning, and did you have the opportunity to discuss this with your Defence team?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I have understood your question, and I have had an opportunity immediately before the beginning of this hearing to talk to my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Am I wrong that this question was already beforehand, and not only immediately before the beginning of this hearing was discussed with your Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with the possible appointment of a new judge, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you are aware of the meaning and the importance of your own decision, and you have no doubts. And if you should have some doubts, and there are remaining questions, this would be the opportunity now to address these questions. Are there any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to expedite the proceedings and bring the trial to a speedy end, and also in order to favour the witnesses who have already appeared here in court, as well as those who were in any way victims of the war, also taking into account the possible extra expenses, I give my full consent for a new judge to be appointed in order not to have to restart the whole trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Stakic. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could only ask, Your Honour, just another thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to kindly ask Your Honour to allow the Defence perhaps between 10 and 15 days more to prepare, and maybe such a period would also be beneficial for the new judge to get better acquainted with this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The question of this issue was already addressed by your Defence counsel, and we'll come back to this later. Let us first proceed step by step, and then see what is really necessary, what are the remaining issues. Thank you. Then this brings me to the next point, and after discussion of the Bench during the last four days, I think it's fair, and it is a must, to inform the parties that in this composition, only one decision will be possible: Either to hand down a decision under 98 bis, or in case there should be a long envisaged agreement among the parties foreseen in the rules as plea bargaining, then there would be a possibility to hand down on the basis of a sentencing hearing the final judgement. But it's really either/or, and it is also only fair to state that there is no remaining time for further discussions. As we said it in the 65 ter meeting, the only appropriate time and the deadline would be today because then the entire procedure, either on 98 bis or a probable sentencing preparation, has to be started. We can't wait any longer. This Trial Chamber, and the three of us, unanimously agreed: Any kind of agreement can be accepted by this Trial Chamber no later than by the end of this day. No doubt, when there in future might be another composition of this Trial Chamber, there might be the possibility of an agreement. But also the parties should know that the mitigating factor of such an agreement decreases day by day and week by week. And the additional value, especially for an accused, is extremely limited when such an agreement is reached only at the end of the case. These are the first two preliminary remarks. First, the first intention is to discuss issues under 98 bis. And in this context, also one clarification is necessary: In some jurisdictions, we have a clear distinction between the Prosecutor's case and then the Defence case. To that end, that after the end of the Prosecution's case, the situation of the accused can no longer be worsened. But as we have a mixture of the both predominant legal systems, it reads, especially in Rule 85(A) that the "Evidence at the trial shall be presented in the following sequence: evidence for the Prosecution; evidence for the Defence; Prosecution evidence in rebuttal; Defence evidence in rejoinder; and then finally evidence ordered by the Trial Chamber pursuant to Rule 98." This means de facto that in case additional evidence is available, be it in favour or not in favour, or even against the interest of the accused, this additional evidence can be ordered by the Trial Chamber. This might emanate from other cases or from a perusal or that what we have heard until now. This makes it more difficult for the Chamber to decide on 98 bis issues because we also have to take into account the likelihood of whether or not additional material can be obtained. The third point is the following -- and here, I informed already the parties because I thought it would be necessary. When discussing the test to be applied, some weeks if not months ago the Chamber cautioned the parties that they shouldn't rely on the jurisprudence, especially expressed in the Djeric Appeals Chamber judgement, saying that the test to apply is whether or not a reasonable trier of fact could come to the conclusion, could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused based on what was heard during the Prosecutor's case. We initially discussed the question whether or not the approach represented in this issue, in an additional opinion by Judge Pocar, would be the correct one, this is whether or not this concrete Trial Chamber could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt. But it follows from that what we heard in the beginning as to the fact that this Chamber might, if necessary, have to continue in another composition, in this case, no doubt, the test can only be the one held in majority in Jelisic, that a reasonable trier of fact could come to such a conclusion. So, what is the purpose, the remaining purpose now? As I said, we have to find out, and we discussed the Prosecutor's case already under this heading, whether a reasonable trier of fact could be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused at this point in time. The word "could" the most important in this context. Now, 98 bis does not only provide for a motion on acquittal of an accused, but it's also possible and foreseen under Rule 98 bis (B) that a Trial Chamber proprio motu or ex officio may enter a judgement of acquittal if it finds that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction on that or those charges. Therefore, it is necessary to point out whether the Chamber tends, in part, to an acquittal; second, to address reasonable doubts that might easily be spelled by comments and arguments of the Prosecutor. And under the special circumstances of this case, I think it's only fair to give also hints in the direction of the Defence to indicate what is this provisional status of the case as of today seen with the eyes of the Judges sitting on this case today. This concludes the preliminary remarks. May I ask: Are there any questions to these provisional remarks?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I'm not entirely clear. Is Your Honour saying that today is the last day on which there could be consideration of Rule 98 submissions? In other words, written submissions -- the timetable for which Your Honour has given will no longer apply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, this would be a misunderstanding. Because as for the motion, if not decided otherwise on the basis of the request expressed by Dr. Stakic in person this morning, no doubt the schedule remains unchanged. Today is only the possibility for the Chamber to express their views and their point under the heading "right to be heard" to the Prosecutor where we either have reasonable doubts or even a tendency to come to an acquittal. It's only from our side. This part, the second part of Rule 98 bis (B) will be addressed during this hearing this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it probably is my fault, Your Honour. What Your Honour is saying is that today is the day for, as Your Honour Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. expressed it, deliberations I suppose. But thereafter, the Trial Chamber will still remain of the composition to make a ruling at the end of the written submissions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I said earlier, there are only two options remaining: Either to proceed under the Rule 98 bis proceedings as envisaged in the scheduling order or, as we discussed during the 65 ter meeting, if the parties so want, today would be the last possible day to try to come to an agreement, once again, under the heading "plea bargaining" as foreseen under the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: These are the options, either/or.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Sorry, it was my misunderstanding. I thought that the Trial Chamber would not be of the same composition after today, but that's not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. May I ask the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, let's come immediately to the core questions. Let's go in medias res. And no doubt, the question of genocide is one of the core questions of this case. The accused is charged with having committed genocide or, alternatively, complicity in genocide. On the basis of the evidence provided until now, there is no reasonable doubt that as regards the objective criteria, genocide has been committed in the entire area, but especially, the substance matter of this case, in the municipality of Prijedor. The main question is whether or not the accused, Dr. Stakic, had the necessary intent to commit this crime. And here, to be quite concrete, the Trial Chamber does not believe that the necessary evidence has been provided to prove this intent or dolus specialis, as it was called in some earlier decisions. We shouldn't go into some details of the definition of what it is, but post, for example, to the dolus evetualis or the dolus directis of first degree, dolus directis of second degree. But the intent -- we are on the basis of what we have heard until now, the intent was not to commit genocide. It was in another direction, more or less. I come back to this later. But we are faced with the additional charge: Complicity in genocide. And here already it is more difficult. Because we don't believe that we have already a settled -- finally settled jurisprudence about the mens rea element as regards complicity in genocide. To go already one step further at this point in time, it appears to be, from a systematical point of view, difficult to find out what the authors of our statute had in mind when, in Article 4, describing what acts shall be punishable, Article 4(3). There it reads: The following acts shall be punishable: Genocide, conspiracy to commit genocide, direct and public incitement to commit genocide, attempt to commit genocide, or complicity in genocide. You read in the indictment, and this follows the earlier forms of the indictment, and also that what you can read in earlier judgements, that at the same time, it is alleged that this was committed under the individual criminal responsibility, Article 7, paragraph 1, where it states that, "A person who planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of a crime referred to in Articles 2 to 5 - we'll say including Article 4 - of the present statute shall be individually responsible for the crime." The question is now, what had the authors of this article in mind when stating "complicity in genocide"? Is it as it is in the normal scope of the definition of the word "complicity" restricted to the coperpetrator, to the accomplice of a crime, or as it was held, for example, in Akayesu, that the aiding and abetting, for example, should -- and the Article 7, should be read into Article 4, paragraph 3 (E). This question still is open. And then the question brings us, and at this point in time, in fact, we can leave it open because it's the position of this Trial Chamber that there might be enough evidence for aiding and abetting to genocide. And then once again the question is what is the necessary mens rea as regards this? And once again, it can be left open whether the decision especially in Akayesu, paragraphs 440 to -- 540 to 547 is the correct approach. Finally, we believe that the mens rea for aiding and abetting, be it only under 7(1) or 7(3) to be read into Article 4, paragraph 3(E). The mens rea for this aiding and abetting would be the knowledge, the taking into account and accepting the results and the outcome, knowing about all the elements of crime of genocide, including the intent of superiors or other persons. And here, indeed, we believe that be it now complicity by knowingly aiding and abetting, sufficient evidence has been provided in principle. We are open for all arguments, no doubt, but the purpose of these deliberations is to invite the parties to discuss these issues. So in conclusion, there is a tendency to acquit as regards genocide as such, but not as regards aiding and abetting to genocide. Before coming to other charges, are there any questions by the parties as regards the question of genocide?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. With respect to the Court's analysis, the Defence certainly - and I'm not sure if this is the appropriate time - takes exception to it. If the Court permits, we would like to discuss the issue of aiding and abetting and also the issue of the necessary requirement of mens rea which is incorporated both in the count 1 of the fourth amended indictment under genocide as well as count 2 under complicity of genocide. Or if the Court would prefer, at the end of Your Honours' deliberations, we can address those issues, or we could address them piecemeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it can be addressed at the end of today's hearings. And probably, it's better to have it in the context, or far better, no doubt, in writing because here we have to go into details, and the purpose of this provisional analysis is only to express our doubts and to express where we see the problems. And at the same time express the direction what we believe has been covered by the evidence provided until now. So either at the end of the deliberations of today or, far better, in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we go into the details of the indictment as regards the other charges and concrete incidents, I want to be aware that I don't know whether this ever was signed. May I ask you, Ms. Korner, I have a draft before me only "Prosecution Notice of the Specific Allegations from the Fourth Amended Indictment which are Conceded as not Proven."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was signed and filed yesterday, sometime during the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence has this document? Fine. Then we are all on the same level. And in addition, that I don't forget this at the end of the day, may I ask the legal officer to distribute what we have prepared on the basis of our compilations. This is two lists. May I ask, could you please give me one copy of each. On the basis of our compilations and with all the necessary reservations that we all are human beings and might have committed the one or other mistake, we have compiled, one, on the basis of the fourth amended indictment a victim list, the annex to this indictment, a list indicating that the Trial Chamber may come to the conclusion that there is insufficient evidence as regards the names that are not highlighted. We'll say that we believe there is not sufficient evidence as regards the names list there had and not highlighted. But at the same time, we have a second list of victims of killings identified by witnesses, but not included in the indictment. And it's for the Office of the Prosecutor to react or not react on these both lists. May they please be distributed to the parties. And just for identification, that we can later come back to this, may I have the next J numbers available.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: J19, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the fourth amended indictment list will be J19, and the list of victims identified by witnesses but not in the indictment will be J20. Let me now turn to one chapeau question, and this is the question on the relationship, but not only the relationship between 7(1) and 7(3). I think as regards this relationship, we have sufficient jurisprudence, and we shouldn't go into details. But as regards 7(3), we have to express some doubts whether under 7(3) enough evidence has been provided. Opposed to 7(1), Article 7 states that: "The fact that any of the acts referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the present statute was committed by a subordinate does not relieve the superior of criminal responsibility if he knew or had reason to know that the subordinate was about to commit such acts or had done so and the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the perpetrators thereof." At first glance, it seems to be surprising that we don't address 7(1) saying that there can be reasonable doubts, but 7(3). This is related to the fact that it clearly states and makes reference to a subordinate. And I think we have a lot of material here available, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the parties are invited to give additional authorities or jurisprudence to that end. But I think it starts with the Celebici judgement, stating in paragraph 378 that it is "necessary that the superior have effective control over the persons committing the underlying violations of international humanitarian law in the sense of having the material ability to prevent and punish the commission of these offences with the caveat that such authority can have a de facto as well as a de jure character. The Trial Chamber, accordingly, shares the view expressed by the International Law Commission that the doctrine of superior responsibility extends to civilian superiors only to the extent that they exercise a degree of control over their subordinates which is similar to that of military commanders." To a certain extent, in Aleksovski judgement, the Judges came to a slightly different definition. They state: "A civilian must be characterised as a superior pursuant to Article 7(3) if he has the ability de jure or de facto to issue orders to prevent an offense and to sanction the perpetrators thereof. A civilian sanction power must however be interpreted broadly. It cannot be expected that a civilian authority will have disciplinary power over his subordinate or equivalent to that of the military authorities in an analogous command position." No doubt, there is a discrepancy between these two definitions. But they continue in the same paragraph, 78: "The Trial Chamber, therefore, considers that the superior's ability de jure or de facto to impose sanctions is not essential. The possibility of transmitting reports to the appropriate authorities suffices once the civilian authority, through its position in the hierarchy, is expected to report whenever crimes are committed and that in the light of his position, the likelihood that those reports will trigger an investigation or initiate disciplinary or even criminal measures is extant." We doubt that also under these conditions, evidence has been given to satisfy us to that extent. And finally, we have to come back to the most recent judgement, that is Kordic. Paragraph 416 where it states: "In some, only those superiors, either de jure or de facto, military or civilian, who are clearly part of a chain of command, either directly or indirectly, with the actual power to control or punish the acts of subordinates may incur criminal responsibility." So in some, we believe the questions whether there is a coordination, whether there's cooperation, is not the right test; the test is whether there was a system of subordination with the consequences just quoted from former judgements. So we have to make a distinction. First, has Dr. Stakic really had such a position of superiority? Had he the possibility to do that what was from different point of views envisaged in former judgements? Or - we also discussed this approach - did the Crisis Staff, as such, as a whole had this superior role? But then we have the question whether or not an individual member of the Crisis Staff can be held responsible because we should bear in mind that Article 7 has a headline "individual criminal responsibility." The question has often been discussed in literature, in jurisprudence whether or not a group can be held responsible, and it's very -- also very specific jurisprudence on the question, for example, whether a court, a Chamber, or a judge, here there are more than one Judges, whether such a group of Judges even can be held responsible for, say, illegal decisions. So this is one crucial aspect. As regards Dr. Stakic himself, we don't believe that sufficient evidence has been presented that he was able, either as it was said in the one decision, to report with the likelihood of sufficient reaction, or to order, say, in the direction of the police or the military forces. As I said, this is a provisional analysis, and we invite the parties to discuss these questions. In addition, we came to the conclusion that when in the indictment it states or it is alleged that Dr. Stakic - and this is true for all charges - is alleged with incitement or instigation, no sufficient evidence seems to be available for this part of the charge. But then we have to go now to the charges as such. And I will follow in the order of the fourth amended indictment. In paragraph 40, we can read that, Dr. Stakic allegedly planned and instigated, and then in the planning and preparation or execution of a campaign and so on. Also here, we believe that there isn't sufficient evidence as to the element of crime "planned and instigated." Different from this, in paragraph 42, we don't believe that there is sufficient evidence for the instigation to exterminate members of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat population in the Prijedor Municipality. And we have to give the hint, and no doubt, it's settled jurisprudence, that if the Trial Chamber would come to the conclusion that a reasonable trier of fact could come to this conclusion, that Dr. Stakic committed such a crime of extermination, then the planning of this would be the included preparation to committing the crime. But we regard it as necessary to concentrate on these alternatives and to concentrate on really applicable alternatives because it's necessary for the preparation of the Defence to know concretely what they have to contest and how they have to establish their case. Turning to paragraph 44, killings, the Prosecution has already withdrawn number 4. As regards number 7, the killing of a number of people in the village of Brisevo on or about 24 July, 1992, it might be difficult to come to the necessary conclusions based on Witness M's testimony only. But here we are open for additional remarks and hints to corroborating evidence. The same holds true for paragraph 46, number 1. As regards the qualification of the Prijedor JNA barracks as a camp, it might be doubtful on the basis of -- to come to this conclusion, on the basis of the testimony of Witness T only. And let me take this point in time to address Dr. Stakic himself. From the point of view of an accused, these going into details may sound strange. You are the only one in the courtroom who, to a certain extent, knows and knew what really happened. But in a criminal case, we have to rely on evidence provided, and there must be, and there may be, a discrepancy between that what we are discussing here and that what you believe as being the truth from your point of view. So we only can express on the -- give our assessment on the basis of the evidence we have at hand. As regards paragraph 47, we wonder if you really have sufficient evidence whether the killing -- for the killing of approximately 50 men and women taken on a bus from Omarska camp in late July 1992, at least some of whose remains were exhumed from Jama Lisac Bosanska Krupa Municipality. As regards paragraph 49, the second paragraph there, it reads in the middle "prominent and educated Bosnian Muslims were subjected to severe beatings and humiliation." In the context of the entire case, we doubt, but are open for additional arguments, that it was really the target that the actions were targeted on prominent and educated Bosnian Muslims, or wasn't it the entire group of Bosnian Muslims as such. And the same holds true as regards paragraph 7 here, when we read "at the JNA barracks, predominantly prominent members of the Bosnian Muslim and Bosnian Croat communities were interrogated and beaten and tortured." We invite the parties to discuss the question whether there is enough and sufficient evidence or not. When we discuss the other charges, count 3, murder, crime against humanity punishable under Articles 5(A), 7(1) and 7(3), we already discussed the question of 7(3). But we don't believe that there is sufficient evidence for any planning, instigation, or ordering. For the count of murder, no doubt, for committing or aiding and abetting, it would be sufficient to have, as regards the mens rea, the knowledge, substantial support, the taking into account of the consequences, and accepting these foreseeable consequences. The word "foreseeable" brings me to that what we in detail discussed among the Judges, and we unanimously came to the conclusion that there is reasonable doubt whether or not that what happened in Room 3 and that what happened at Mount Vlasic was in the scope of foreseeability or whether or not it was a deviation from an alleged criminal plan. Paragraph 54, and there under (3)(ix), this incident was already dropped by the Prosecution. We have some doubts whether we have sufficient evidence for the destruction. The willful damage and looting of Donja and Gornja Ravska and Kevljani. Also here we invite comments. Under (B), we know now that we came to the same assessment, as where (i) and (ii) has been dropped and forms no longer part of this indictment. As regards count 6, persecution, crimes against humanity, we do believe that among the alternatives quoted in the indictment, there is a tendency to committing. As said earlier, the planning and ordering can be regarded as the included preparation to committing. Finally, we come to count 8, and this is a very special problem. It's a question of principle. You know that for good reasons in the book of authorities we find the remarks that what is laid down in our statute, in Article 5(I), are they inhumane acts, whether this additional alternative is in line with the fundamental principles of criminal law. Here, the principle of clarity and definitiveness. There are serious problems with this because, indeed, it is extremely vague what is meant by "other inhumane acts." This is already the first observation. And the second is -- isn't the alleged, under this heading, the alleged forcible transfer part of deportation? And second, is it relevant for the outcome Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of this case? Therefore, unanimously, the Judges would ask the OTP whether or not it's possible to drop count 8 for the given reasons. This concludes the remarks from the side of the Bench. While the parties are thinking about their possible comments, if any, I have to come back to the Prosecution's Notice of Specific Allegations from the Fourth Amended Indictment which are Conceded as Not Proven, under 5, it states, "For the foregoing reasons the Prosecution requests that the Trial Chamber permit the Prosecution to withdraw the specific allegations as described in paragraphs 2 to 4 above." Formally, I have to ask the Defence, are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the permission is given. Do any of the parties want to make at this point in time comments, or has any of the parties reason to put questions to that what I tried to explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on -- Mr. Koumjian wants to make some factual comments on some of the things you've raised, but I think the onus, because it is Rule 98, effectively is on the Defence to deal with it first if they have any comments to make because we're responding effectively to their application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You started already earlier. But now the floor is yours for at least the next 20 minutes to address the issues, if necessary. Of course we can continue after a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I disagree with my learned friend Ms. Korner that the onus is on the Defence, and I think that a review, whether it's detailed or cursory, of the fourth amended indictment clearly reflects that the OTP does not want to have the burden of proof to be placed on them, but has instead chosen to shift that burden and have attempted throughout the proceedings to shift the burden to the Defence. Nevertheless, we'll accept the offer to go first in this case, and would like to at least raise some questions with the Chamber, if permitted. Specifically, I think when reviewing the fourth amended indictment, one comes to the immediate conclusion that there are both cumulative and duplicitous charges within the indictment. Each of the eight counts clearly reflect that unnecessary and prohibited alternative theory that the Prosecutor seeks against Dr. Stakic. They must choose, and we are of the opinion the law in this jurisprudence requires them to choose, whether or not the charges against Dr. Stakic are premised upon either 7(1), individual responsibility, or 7(3), command responsibility. The Celebici Appeals Chamber clearly noted in agreeing with the OTP that it is difficult at times to conclude with certainty which evidence may be forthcoming and which evidence is significant. When read closely, the Appeals Chamber in Celebici used the words "prior to the presentation of evidence." The OTP has rested. It is their day in court where they must, in our opinion, based on the decisional authority in this Tribunal, make an appropriate election. They cannot expect the Defence to argue alternative theories. They must be able to at some point decide whether their evidence was sufficient to conclude that Dr. Stakic has individual responsibility or command responsibility. They have not done so, even though the Chamber has invited them by today's deadline to make that submission. Specifically with respect to 7(3) and the command responsibility, the two alternative theories within that section, de jure and de facto, clearly permit that individual responsibility under the very term de facto falls within that section. Comparatively speaking, when you make the analysis to 7(1), there must be some affirmative action done by an individual for him to be found criminally liable under individual responsibility. The OTP cannot make up their mind. In our opinion, respectfully, for obvious reasons because they don't believe, in our opinion, that they have sustained sufficient factual backdrop by way of both lay witnesses who have appeared before the Court as well as, as they have called them, expert witnesses presented before the Chamber. We believe that the Defence will be prejudiced significantly if the OTP does not make that choice. And they should be required to make it before the submissions of Rule 98 bis, and certainly they should make them today. With respect to the issue of counts 1 and 2, we believe as the OTP well knows, the jurisprudence in this Tribunal, that the lesser offence, namely, complicity in genocide, clearly denotes a special intent is necessary. By not requiring this special intent, we believe, will only render the theory of liability of conspiracy to commit genocide to that of persecution which also in and of itself has a distinct and separate mens rea element known commonly as discriminatory intent through some of the authority provided by the Tribunal. There cannot be in discussions of genocide a modification in our respectful view to this specific special intent. Whether we call it under Article 4(3)(A), (B), (C), (D), or (E), (E) being complicity in genocide. Each and every one of those specific charges require special and specific intent. The Court noted aiding and abetting as cited in the Krstic case, which I believe they incorporated the definition from Aleksovski, aiding and abetting means the rendering of a substantial contribution to the commission of a crime. Again, the OTP has not provided any evidence through any of their expert witnesses to indicate that there was, in our opinion, contribution, much less the significant substantial contribution. We agree with the Court's view with respect to count 8, specifically the jurisprudence has found that deportation and forcible transfer are defined separately. The OTP again has chosen to make alternative arguments under count 7, namely, deportation, and counts 8, which is what they consider other inhumane acts. We suggest that both should be viewed, and the specific jurisprudence found that there was no, in our opinion, prima facie evidence to suggest or to meet count 7 of their fourth amended complaint -- indictment. As the Court well knows, when we discuss deportation, it is the exodus of citizens from one state to another. I dare say, from my recollection and review of the transcripts and the testimony of the witnesses, that there was not one witness who stated that there was this significant deportation of citizens from one state to another. We also believe that in order for there to be this criminal enterprise, or as the OTP likes to refer to it, as a joint criminal enterprise, that they must set forth specifically what that enterprise was. They must also, we believe, identify what was the widespread and systematic pattern and attack. We believe they failed to do that. And upon their analysis of the facts, we believe they should, in order to provide the Defence with the adequate opportunity to bring their witnesses, not only make a decision, but we expect them to concede that those fundamental elements have not been proven by any of their witnesses. In fact, from one of their quasi-experts who testified - and when I use that word, he was an expert in prior cases - to establish the very element of widespread and systematic, that the OTP in our opinion wisely decided not to use the individual as an expert in this case, not only because he wasn't qualified to give such testimony then or now, but because his very own articles clearly and unequivocally suggest that there was not widespread and systematic attack. We would like the opportunity as the Court has given us, and we thank the Court in advance, to be able to address all these issues within our 98 bis submission. Finally, if I may add, with respect to 98 bis (B), clearly the sufficiency of the evidence is contemplated by the very language within that rule and provision which requires, in our opinion, that the Court not just accept a factual backdrop of something a witness gives but is required under the law to weigh, to assess, and to clearly make a determination as to whether the evidence provided by those witnesses are substantial and significant wherein another Trial Chamber may be able to make that evaluation. In our view, since the three Honourable Judges before us were able to assess the credibility of the witnesses, and since the decisional authority clearly finds that if an essential ingredient in a crime is missing, that a Trial Chamber may acquit, we believe that on significant items, the specific ingredient of the crime was missing as it relates specifically to Dr. Stakic despite their alternative theories. We also believe that it is respectfully this Trial Chamber's assessment of all the evidence that must be considered in determining whether or not to acquit Dr. Stakic of the numerous cumulative counts. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your comments and observations. Only one point should be addressed now: Under Rule 98 bis (B), there are, as I stated earlier, two alternatives: The motion of an accused to be expected and a decision proprio motu. And what we did today was, as it is demanded by the Appeals Chamber in the Jelisic appeal judgement, the right to be heard. This means that we have to indicate where we have our doubts, where we tend to an acquittal. And the silence means that there are no doubts as the evidence stands as of today; and in addition, I think we pointed out where there is a tendency where we would come to an acquittal, also as regards the alternatives within one and the same charge in order to be as concrete as possible to facilitate the Defence to prepare their case. But it's never foreseen, and it's nowhere foreseen, that it's for the Prosecution immediately to respond. So therefore, it's for the Prosecution to decide whether they want to address the one or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. other issue today or put the proprio motu argument together with the motion of an accused. And I think this is what we can expect. But indeed, we support the view that it would be of assistance to be more concrete and to concentrate on the core issues of this case. And therefore, we also touched upon issues normally not to be addressed at this point in time already. Please, the floor is yours for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, we're very grateful to Your Honour for the -- I think the word used originally was judicial hints that we have been given today. It does assist. I'm going to allow -- Mr. Koumjian is going to address Your Honours on a few of the factual matters that Your Honour has raised, and the evidence, just touch on some of the evidence we say is there. I just want to deal with the submission made just by Mr. Ostojic, that it was incumbent upon us to elect between 7(1) liability and 7(3) liability today. Your Honour, that is a complete and utter misreading of the decision in Celebici. I would refer Mr. Ostojic to paragraphs 743 onwards in the judgement which made it absolutely clear that there can be a conviction on both 7(1) and 7(3). There is no onus on the Prosecution to elect. And indeed, if there is a finding of guilt on both 7(1) and 7(3), the Trial Chamber is obliged to take that into account as an aggravating factor in sentencing on whichever, usually 7(1). So there's no need for us to elect. Secondly, Your Honour, can I just mention why there is the charge, which is count 8, of inhumane acts, transfer. That is because there is a difference between deportation and transfer, as Your Honour knows, and that's the reason why there are two counts. But we take into account what Your Honours have to say about that. Mr. Koumjian would wish to address Your Honour on some of the factual matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But I think it's appropriate to have the necessary break now. And therefore, the trial stays adjourned until 12.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Koumjian, please, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to just address a few of the issues that Your Honour pointed out and directed our attention to this morning. I'm doing this somewhat off the top of my head, and I will be directing Your Honours to specific evidence that I recall that related to these points. In our written brief, we will be much more detailed both to citing the evidence and where it appears in the transcript and also in addressing legal questions. My purpose now is just to give a few -- an overview of the few points that we think are directly related to important aspects of the proof regarding issues that Your Honours highlighted this morning. One of the points raised this morning was the responsibility of Dr. Stakic for decisions by the Crisis Staff which was itself a group of individuals. Your Honour pointed out that issue when we -- the Tribunal seeks to hold persons individually responsible, how do we hold people responsible for decisions by a group? But obviously, if we follow this logic to its ultimate conclusion, one could say that no one is responsible when a group, a small group such as the Crisis Staff, makes decisions. In fact, we think in this case, there has been evidence that Dr. Stakic not only was completely voluntary in his participation in the decisions of the Crisis Staff, but that the evidence shows Dr. Stakic's unique and important role in the decisions of the Crisis Staff. You recall, Your Honours, early in the trial we played a video where there was an interview with Colonel Arsic. Colonel Arsic was asked to discuss the situation in Prijedor, and he indicated that it's because he was so well acquainted. He said not only was he well acquainted but all the civilian authorities, he makes it a point to make them acquainted. There followed an interview with Dr. Stakic. I believe the journalist was Mr. Rade Mutic, and he was introduced. He introduced Dr. Stakic as the first man of the municipality. And this has been the evidence consistently throughout the trial. Even to the witness Mr. Baltic who when asked by Mr. Lukic about the responsibility and role of Dr. Stakic said "the title, president of the municipality, speaks for itself." He was the number one in Prijedor, and particularly during the time of the Crisis Staff; he was the president of the Crisis Staff. He was also the highest ranking SDS member on the Crisis Staff because the president was not a member, but Dr. Stakic, as the vice-president of the SDS, was the highest SDS member of the Crisis Staff. We know from the evidence presented in this case that Dr. Stakic spoke in the name of the Crisis Staff. We have presented evidence where he spoke to the local press. You recall the one short video interview where Dr. Stakic was discussing the attack on Kozarac, and what he said, the military -- what the military called the cleansing or Ciscenje. We know that he spoke to the international press and made efforts on behalf of the Crisis Staff and others, other members of this joint criminal enterprise, in our view, to keep the international attention or international press, to keep their attention off of Prijedor and off of the horrible crimes that were happening in particular the camps. They were successful all the way up until August the 5th when Penny Marshall and a few other journalists were able to go to the camps and to report what was happening. I think the evidence shows how important that was because the situation changed dramatically after that. The killings that were everyday occurrences soon diminished, and the camps were closed. Shortly after, what was happening in Prijedor became known to the world. Dr. Stakic did his best to make sure this was not known to the world. We also have presented evidence in documents that decisions of the Crisis Staff were signed by Dr. Stakic. You recall the interview of Dr. Stakic that is in evidence, the longer one. It is about a 45-minute interview. I'm sorry I don't have the S number off the top of my head where Dr. Stakic was asked about his role, and he said first he was president of the municipality. And secondly, he was asked then, Is that like the mayor? And he said, Yes, precisely that. And he was asked about his role, and he said he signed the orders of the Crisis Staff. And in fact, the evidence is overwhelming that it is Dr. Stakic's order -- excuse me, signature on many of these orders, the rather unique manner of signing S. Milomir, the same manner of signing a last initial, first name, that was on documents found on his person at the time of his arrest. Finally, Dr. Stakic had the very, very crucial role, both as president of the Crisis Staff and president of the municipality of setting the agenda. It was his unique role to set the agenda for the meetings, for the discussion, for the decisions of the Crisis Staff. That is confirmed both by the statute and by Mr. Baltic's testimony who indicated it is the president of the municipality who set the agenda. Dr. Stakic presided over the meetings of both the Municipal Assembly and of the Crisis Staff. So the evidence in this case shows that Dr. Stakic was much more than a member of this Crisis Staff. He played a unique and critical role. Many of these same factors that I have just listed are also relevant to the other issue Your Honour highlighted and directed our attention to and that is the evidence of a de facto or de jure authority by Dr. Stakic under Article 7(3) of those who actually physically perpetrated the crimes. His role as the number one man in the municipality is relevant to this discussion. In addition, we have in this case orders. We have signed orders to the police and army that we know were complied with. If the issue is, can this man give an order to an army and the police, the answer is yes because we know from the documents that, for example, the Crisis Staff ordered the intervention squad to be set up, and in fact indicated that they would have approve the members. We have a Crisis Staff order to the army and police to provide security at the hospital. To the army, we have a Crisis Staff decision naming the logistics commander. Another Crisis Staff decision replacing Slobodan Kuruzovic as the head of the TO. We have -- we admit we have much stronger evidence on the police than we do on the army. On the police, we have, for example, the document that Dr. Baltic sent to Mr. Drljaca asking him to indicate how -- whether or not the decisions of the Crisis Staff had been implemented by the police and how they were implemented. And we have the response by Mr. Drljaca. We know that, for example, the Crisis Staff ordered that illegally acquired property be returned -- excuse me, not be returned, be given to the municipality. I forget the exact words used, but that the municipality would confiscate illegally acquired property. That's property that was stolen. It is very interesting that nowhere does the Crisis Staff order that this stolen property be returned to those it was stolen from. We know that many, many houses, personal property, cars were confiscated, and Muslim or a Croat could not drive a car in Prijedor and expect to keep it. The Crisis Staff did nothing about that. The Crisis Staff -- we have some decisions and orders and Kozarski Vjesnik articles asking the police to stop the looting of businesses, and it appears from the totality of the evidence talking about Serbian-owned businesses. Could the Crisis Staff punish individuals? Well, we have absolutely clear evidence of that. They punished, they detained, they put into camps thousands of people. Muslims and Croats. If the Crisis Staff could order the detention of Muslims and Croats, then clearly they had the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. power to order the arrest and detention of other Serb perpetrators. If the Crisis Staff could order that the president, legitimately elected, of the municipality, President Cehajic, be arrested, and sign an order that no one would be released from the camps without their permission, then clearly the Crisis Staff had the power to punish and prevent the crimes that were occurring. And in fact, the Crisis Staff did, in the end, do something to stop the crimes, not because they wanted to but because of the international spotlight. And that is after the visit of the international journalists, the camps were closed. That itself shows the power of the Crisis Staff to prevent crimes. I'd like to brief address the Room 3 and Vlasic mountain massacres and their relationship to the criminal conduct of the accused. Your Honours, it's our position that we do not have to show for foreseeability that the accused knew the exact time and the exact place where a crime would be committed. But it is our view that from the totality of the evidence, it was clear that a campaign of persecutions including killings was going on in Prijedor. Extremely prominent individuals had been detained, extremely prominent individuals known to the accused had been killed in the camps including a great many of his fellow physicians, including his former boss, the president of the municipality, the person who had an office directly across from him, the person who he replaced. We saw the video of Dr. Stakic talking about Kozarac and the great victory of the army there, while at the same time we could see in that video house after house destroyed and burning. We saw what the road -- some short shots of what the road looked like and we heard evidence that Kozarac was destroyed, not in a military attack but following the attack. Fires were set, grenades were thrown into houses. Kozarac was destroyed. We know that Stari Grad was destroyed - the old part of Prijedor - and razed to the ground, bulldozed to the ground. We know from the witnesses who testified that in July, the Brdo area was attacked, and one village after another was cleansed, as the army said. There was a Ciscenje in those villages. And we saw from the witnesses who survived those that what that meant, it meant deporting to Trnopolje the women and children, killing many of the men, putting the remainder of the men into camps like Omarska and Keraterm. One of those groups of people from the Brdo area were those that were put into Room 3. Given what had happened in the Brdo where village after village was attacked, was cleansed, where killings occurred with complete impunity. All this time, from late May until the Room 3 massacre in late July, many hundreds, thousands of killings had occurred with complete impunity given that it certainly was not unforeseeable. In fact, we think it certainly is foreseeable that a crime such as Room 3 and Vlasic mountain would occur. Room 3 massacre the evidence showed was not something done on the spur of the moment. There was a machine-gun set up outside that room. These were people from the Brdo area who had been treated particularly harshly from the moment they arrived at the camp. And then if we look at the Vlasic mountain massacre, again, this was not something done by one or two individuals. This was done by a group. This was a convoy of well over a thousand individuals. There were at least ten perpetrators actually at the scene. Both of these crimes we had many bodies. In Room 3, the bodies had to be disposed of. In both of these crimes it would have been extremely easy at the time to identify the perpetrators if there was any intention to do so. The evidence shows clearly that in Prijedor, under Dr. Stakic in 1992, to kill a Muslim or a Croat was not a crime. You could do so with impunity. There was no sign of disapproval by the authorities or by Dr. Stakic to those killings. And given that, it's not surprising that a crime also like Vlasic mountain where over 200 men are lined up on a cliff and massacred occurs. Again, it would have been so easy to identify the perpetrators of the Vlasic mountain massacre. It would be very easy to know which police officers were escorting that convoy. There was no intent to do so, to punish or to prevent. The only intent by the authorities and by Dr. Stakic was to cover up the crimes that had occurred because Dr. Stakic was very much involved in those crimes from the beginning. He was responsible for that campaign of persecutions and we believe he knew so. I'd like to briefly address now the evidence regarding instigation and planning. Your Honours, first of all, it is our belief that the law of the Tribunal does not require at this stage a 98 bis hearing, that the -- either the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber identify the mode of responsibility. And certainly, it's possible, and it has happened in other cases, that an Appeals Chamber finds a different mode of responsibility. Certainly, there's also many cases where the Trial Chamber found a different mode of responsibility than that principally advanced by the Prosecution. But I'd like to address particularly the instigation and planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Koumjian, before you proceed, I know it seems to be impolite, but for personal reasons, may I ask you for a break of about 5 minutes. And then we continue immediately. Thank you. --- Break taken at 12.23 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding. And sorry for the interruption. Please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We do believe that there is evidence that a reasonable Trial Chamber could find proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused both instigated and planned crimes in the fourth amended indictment. Regarding instigation, we have presented in evidence a certain number, admittedly, a limited number of documents concerning public statements of the accused, again both in B/C/S to the local population, and also public statements to the international community. Dr. Stakic continually portrayed his enemies -- portrayed as enemies Muslims and Croats, particularly, though, Muslims in Prijedor. He described a threat that he said was coming from being directed from Tehran and the Vatican. Again, he denied the existence of the camps or tried to misportray what was actually going on in those camps. He talked about the people of Prijedor or the Serbian population of Prijedor facing a jihad. And he continually referred to the importance of avoiding another Jasenovac, another -- the camp where so many Serbs had been killed in Croatia during World War II, continually brought up the experience, the horrible experience and suffering of the Serbian people in World War II, and tried to portray the neighbours in Prijedor who were of Muslim and Croat ethnicity as being threats to the Serbian population and as being threats to commit -- threatening to commit another genocide, when in fact there was no evidence of that. Similarly, the evidence shows planning on the part of Dr. Stakic and his associates. We know that prior to the takeover, arms were being distributed among the Serbian population. And that once the takeover occurred, the next step was the disarmament of the non-Serbian population. This was done neighbourhood by neighbourhood, village by village on the orders of the Crisis Staff. We know that people were arrested according to lists, and we even know that in the camps, there were lists that were used when people were killed. Guards would come at night with a list of names. We know that also, for example, I believe it was August 5th when Keraterm was closed, the commander read out the names of a hundred or so, 100 or 120, individuals who were placed on two buses and never seen again. And some of the remains were exhumed from Hrastova Glavica. Prior to the attacks or the Ciscenje, the cleansing of villages, there clearly was planning in how artillery was positioned. Even the initial attacks on Hambarine and Kozarac, it's clear that guns were positioned facing in position to fire artillery barrages on those communities. The deportations were carried out in a methodical fashion. The Crisis Staff paid for the buses. We have the bills from Autotransport Prijedor, and the authority of the Crisis Staff for those buses to deport individuals or to forcibly transfer them to the territory controlled by the Muslim or Sarajevo government forces. The most obvious example of the planning were the camps. The camps were set up on the orders of the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff also controlled the camps in that it indicated no one could be released without their order. There was directions to the military to provide security of the perimeter. There's many, many more examples, and I don't want to list all of them -- or I probably could not off the top of my head. But I think what the evidence shows in particular with Prijedor, and the horrible things that happened in Prijedor, is that Prijedor presented a problem for those who were planning on a Serbian state or Republika Srpska in that Prijedor was a community with a Muslim plurality. Serbs were a minority; they were -- they even -- they were second -- the Muslims had a plurality, and it appeared, a growing population. The government of -- I think Prijedor was the only, the evidence was from Dr. Mujadzic, the only Krajina Municipality to elect a Muslim government. So Prijedor created a particular problem for those planning on a -- the separation of peoples and the creation of a Serbian state. And in that planning, it became very important that Prijedor be cleansed, and that the cleansing that was planned was a particularly brutal one for that particular municipality. Your Honour, I just want to briefly address a couple of the paragraphs that Your Honour mentioned, and not all of them. I'll just direct Your Honours and Your Honours' staff to some of the evidence we believe will appear in the transcript at this point. Regarding the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cleansing -- or excuse me, the attack on Brisevo, we would ask Your Honours to look at the testimony Mr. Ivo Atlija who testified regarding the attack on that village. And in regards to paragraph 47, and I believe Your Honour directed us to paragraph 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 5 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Regarding paragraph 5, we would ask Your Honours to direct your attention to the 92 bis statement of Witness T. Witness T talked about his mother being placed on those buses, along with -- and I think he gave a figure of 40-odd individuals, and there is evidence regarding the exhumation of some individuals named in a particular location and their identification. Again, thank you for the opportunity to address you. I just wanted to hit a few highlights of our views on the issues raised by Your Honours this morning. And we will respond in more depth, particularly regarding the legal issues, in our written submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to express also on behalf of my colleagues the extreme gratitude that once again you highlighted your point of view as regards both facts and including also legal issues. I think under the prevailing exceptional circumstances, it is adequate and appropriate to exchange arguments already at this point in time in order that all the parties know where we stand, where the Prosecution stands, and I can only invite, if they so want, the Defence also to give some additional comments that we have the entire picture before we come to the remaining question of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence believes that the Prosecution is trying to paint with a rather broad brush and that it should not be permitted because the evidence does not substantiate specifically that what was just stated; namely, that Dr. Stakic had a boss, specifically that Dr. Stakic ordered the arrest of the late Mr. Cehajic. I would like the OTP to show us the evidence concrete as required based upon their burden of proof, whether it's documentary evidence or through lay witnesses. They have not done that. The inference they would like us all to draw is always against the accused, Dr. Stakic. Painting with a broad brush is not what is required by them under their burden of proof. They must be specific; they must bring forth the exact evidence in order to substantiate any and all allegations. They identified things like signing orders to the police and the army. Show us the concrete evidence where Dr. Stakic ordered that there be either deportation, expulsion, or any crime including murder to be committed upon any ethnic group, Muslim or Croat. In the opening statements when the trial commenced on the 16th of April of this year, Ms. Joanna Korner was specific in stating and utilising the word "aiding and abetting." They would like to transform the definition of instigation and planning, and they try to utilise that by inflaming the facts and by pointing through their exhumation evidence the tragic and unnecessary deaths that occurred. Their only expert who could show that there was either 7(1) or 7(3) responsibility was the military expert. He conceded both in his oral direct examination through the Power Point presentation that there was a cooperation between the military and police as well as coordination. He conceded, however, that his analysis was rather limited with respect to the civilian authorities and the police. Interestingly, the OTP concedes that they have a vast amount of evidence against the police. Which witness established any link whatsoever between the civilian authorities and the MUP? Which witness established for the Court with any clarity what the hierarchical structure was of the police in Prijedor, much less how it may relate to the civilian authorities? The inference under the law and jurisprudence of this Tribunal is to favour the accused, Dr. Stakic, for they have not only failed to meet their burden of proof; they cannot because no such proof exists, and all they have is mere argument with respect to those issues. Argument, in our opinion, respectfully, made of whole cloth. When they highlight for the Court the videos that were played, I would ask the Court to note the date and the time the videos were played, and also take the exhibit wherein Mr. Simo Drljaca gives a report whether through a three-month or nine-month analysis of what occurred. Read the report as to what Mr. Drljaca claims were the number of deaths that occurred in Prijedor. If it's true what the Prosecution states, that Drljaca informed them, we must examine on the next step what information was provided. That report does not give an accurate portrayal of what occurred. That report suggests, and I believe establishes, that Dr. Stakic was indeed left in the dark as to what was occurring and was not being informed as to what had happened or what would happen on the terrain. The Prosecution, although, seems to indicate that there's a foreseeability issue with respect to Room 3 and Mount Vlasic. We submit respectfully that same natural and foreseeable consequence should and indeed must, according to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, be applied with respect to that which occurred on May 22nd at Hambarine as well as that which occurred on May 24th at Kozarac. Were the civilian authorities notified that a Muslim checkpoint was going to attack a military personnel killing two, wounding four? Were the civilian authorities notified on the 24th of May that a Muslim checkpoint with armed men were going to attack and kill a convoy passing through on the Banja Luka/Prijedor Road? Did the military contact the civilian authorities to request permission to retaliate, to attack, or even to go beyond the normal rules of engagement? We heard from the OTP's witness. We heard what it means to clear a semi-urban and an urban area when he unequivocally said - and I'm paraphrasing - that he understands to clear an area is to capture it and to destroy or kill everyone within. Thankfully, Mr. Brown was not there during those attacks. Admittedly, the military went beyond what was necessary in both those attacks. However, the responsibility is not, as suggested by the OTP, with the civilian authorities; it stands with the military. If they have strong evidence against the police, I wonder how they would quantify the evidence against the military. It's rather offensive to hear, quite frankly, that under Dr. Stakic in 1992 to kill a Muslim or a Croat was not a crime. That statement in and of itself enlightens us not only as to how broad they would like to paint the evidence, but how narrowly they view the statements made by Dr. Stakic throughout the critical period. As we remember his statement, on May 12th, 1992, at a Serbian session that Dr. Stakic is asking for peace. At no time is there any evidence, whether it's documentary or through lay or expert witnesses, which would suggest that Dr. Stakic had any discriminatory intent or any intent whatsoever to justify a comment or to suggest that there's any evidence that to kill a Muslim or a Croat was not a crime. Did the OTP present evidence, concrete evidence, to establish that a civilian authority, a local politician, was able to interfere with any of the hierarchical structures, whether police or military? They did not. Why? None exists. There was no responsibility under Article 7(3), and there was no authority by which Dr. Stakic could interfere. But then again, we want to paint with a broad brush and say that one individual man 29 years old at the time surrounded by experienced elder statesmen in a municipality was able to not only manipulate the events that occurred, but that indeed he was able to control all of them. Such evidence is not before the Tribunal; such evidence does not exist simply because that was not the reality then and it certainly is not the reality now. The OTP spends some time on instigation and planning. They cite for instigation documents public statements to the local population. I invite them to point at any time when Dr. Stakic made a statement which would have been considered not only discriminatory but even defamatory during the critical time period as the OTP chooses, up through August 5th, 1992. Public statements to the international press? I thought we heard that. I thought their witness from the international press told us not only in 1992, but in 1997, and in 2002 he was of the opinion that the late Dr. Kovacevic was in control and in charge. With respect to planning, there's a claim that there's arms distribution. We've seen no such evidence that Dr. Stakic at any time ordered, assisted, or planned that there be an arms distribution to Serbs in the Prijedor Municipality. The orders that we do see with respect to disarmament as asked by specific witnesses, as Dr. Brown shared with us, the orders clearly say that all illegal weapons for all people in the municipality should be turned over. I believe that the Court will, and we are confident that the Court will examine the evidence in its totality, will weigh the evidence of witnesses who in our opinion have not only contradicted themselves on numerous occasions, but witnesses who have appeared here and have been inconsistent with what was said in their direct examination and that which was offered during cross-examination. We also would like to thank the opportunity -- or thank the Chamber for giving us an opportunity to address you in our 98 bis submissions, and we appreciate the time that was given to us this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to thank you as well for these clear words. I think it's now not the time to go into far more details because this has to be done very, very carefully analysing the documents word by word and analysing the jurisprudence and other authorities in depth. We indicated earlier where the problems may lie from our point of view; and given the special circumstances of the case, let me now address that what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I repeatedly did in the past, to emphasise the specific value to come to consensual solution as foreseen under Rule 65 -- 62 bis of our rules. And I think already in the past, but also especially this morning, Dr. Stakic showed, himself, cooperation, cooperation which not is self-understanding. From my experience, at this point, that's the day where the Defence or the accused tries to use the concrete situation to come to a solution under these special circumstances. And using - I don't want to make use of the word "abusing" - this special situation. Therefore, we have to take into account this spirit of cooperation. I think this hearing has served also to meet the prerequisites, the formal prerequisites, under Rule 62 bis. I don't want to touch in detail on Roman I. No doubt, and this has to be emphasised to you, Dr. Stakic, that such a guilty plea has to be made, if so, voluntarily and this voluntarity [sic] must be also not equivocal. So therefore, if you should decide not to plea, then this is your right, no doubt. But more important is II. It's not only under 98 bis, but also under 62 bis that the accused, that Dr. Stakic, is informed, and I think the contributions by all parties and the Judges hopefully as well served for giving this information where we are at this point in time. And when conferring in the meantime with my Honourable Colleagues, we don't believe that much has changed as regards the value of, if any, a crime committed by Dr. Stakic. So it shall serve as a basis for a decision whether or not to enter such a plea. And it is also serves to indicate whether or not the parties and the Judges believe that there is sufficient factual basis for the crime and the accused's participation in it, as we can read it in Rule 62 bis, IV. So in conclusion, I believe it's especially important at this point in time for the Defence to know about the provisional assessment by this Chamber. And I have to emphasise once more: This Chamber unfortunately deplorable in this composition will not be available any longer for the purpose to accept a plea under Rule 62 bis; if not, at least we can find a starting point. It doesn't mean that we have to fix -- the parties have to fix such an agreement already today. But we have to identify today whether or not there is a likelihood to come to such an agreement foreseen under Rule 62 bis. We all know that we are in this special situation for unforeseeable and deplorable reasons. But I believe all the parties and the Tribunal should regard this point in time as a unique chance to come to a fair, balanced, and maybe never-again-achievable solution today. For the Tribunal, this special value is without any doubt that we are under the obligation to act as effectively as possible, to act in a fair and expeditious way. Already in the beginning of this trial, I emphasised that the notion of a fair trial includes, no doubt, an expeditious trial. And let me please invite the parties under these very special circumstances to reconsider what is possible for them; and as it was already said in the 65 ter (I) meeting, I have available already and signed this document on the minutes of the 65 ter (I) meeting, and for the purposes to have a better basis, it should be distributed as soon as possible to the parties. I want to, as is stated there, invite one representative of both parties to my office this afternoon, 3.00. And for the reasons laid down in this strictly confidential document. May it please be distributed as soon as possible to the parties. And this can only have an appellant function. As regards Dr. Stakic, the main person in this case, please take into account that as mentioned, this is indeed a unique chance for very, very special reasons. And this chance will never come back. The trial stays adjourned until further notice.
